Dermatology · published research

Acrodermatitis continua

A single case report describes improvement after polarized broadband light was added for refractory acrodermatitis continua. The report is a clinical observation rather than a controlled estimate of treatment effect.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

One pregnancy case report describes improvement after polarized broadband light was added for refractory acrodermatitis continua.

Summary of the Evidence

One pregnancy case described marked improvement after polarized, broadband light was added for refractory acrodermatitis continua. The report is the only direct clinical observation identified for this condition.

Human and clinical evidence

The case describes substantial improvement after a potent topical corticosteroid had not controlled the lesions. The patient received polarized, polychromatic noncoherent light, with improvement reported after four sessions and maintained during the reported follow-up. The authors reported no treatment-related adverse effect (Choi et al. 2011).

Animal evidence

No animal study specific to acrodermatitis continua was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The report used polarized broadband light at a fluence of 10 J/cm², delivered once or twice weekly. This polychromatic source is not a single red or near-infrared wavelength. The report does not compare alternative wavelengths, doses, or schedules (<a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21394319/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Choi et al. 2011</a>).

Interpretation

The case records improvement in one patient after polarized light was introduced. It cannot determine how often patients respond or whether the same result occurs with other devices or treatment schedules.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Very low for improvement in acrodermatitis continua.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

The evidence is one uncontrolled case report in a pregnant patient. The reported improvement followed treatment with polarized broadband light, but natural fluctuation and concurrent care cannot be separated from the light exposure. There is no independent replication or controlled comparison, so the likelihood and size of benefit cannot be estimated (Choi et al. 2011).
